assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Z2 topological insulator is a genuinely new state of matter: the Kane-Mele proposal of the quantum spin Hall state, its experimental realisation in HgTe wells, and the subsequent three-dimensional topological insulators with protected surface states. It gave condensed matter a new organising principle, with spectroscopic signatures (ARPES, transport) that theory predicts quantitatively and that are very amenable to first-principles electronic-structure work. It followed the 2016 prize for topological phase transitions without duplicating it.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the decisive theory (Z2 invariant, spin-orbit-driven quantum spin Hall state); Molenkamp's group delivered the first experimental demonstration in HgTe/CdTe following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and Fu with Kane for 3D, are not in the credited names, and Hasan's ARPES work on 3D TIs is a competing claim; Kane, Mele and Molenkamp gives the most coherent theory-plus-experiment trio from the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Nearly two decades of independent confirmation across many materials and groups, with a stable interpretation. Timing is ripe or even somewhat late; the field has spawned quantum anomalous Hall and many spin-off phases.
uncertainties: Attribution is genuinely contested: Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Fu are outside the supplied credit, and Hasan's 3D experimental role is excluded by the trio chosen.
I have not independently verified the precise priority chronology of the HgTe prediction versus observation.
Practical impact is so far modest compared with the conceptual impact.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a new platform in which flat bands produce correlated insulators and superconductivity with tunable twist and gating. It is a vivid example of experiment surprising theorists and links to electronic-structure theory (continuum and ab initio models of moire bands). Impact on 2D quantum materials and moire physics has been very large and rapid.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat band at the magic angle (2011); Jarillo-Herrero's group observed correlated insulators and superconductivity (2018), with Cao as lead author, who is not credited. Other groups (Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov and others) contributed in key ways, so the three-person configuration omits significant experimental work and is imperfect.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by many groups across several moire systems, but the superconducting mechanism and the nature of the correlated states remain debated. Only about eight years since discovery, so timing may be early.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism and the complete phase diagram are unresolved.
Sample-to-sample variability and twist-angle disorder complicate interpretation.
Whether the Committee considers the field mature enough is uncertain, and credit allocation among experimental groups is disputed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magnetic skyrmions are topologically protected spin textures observed in chiral magnets and later at interfaces, with deep connections to Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya physics, topological Hall effect and low-current-density spin-torque motion. It sits squarely in my own field of magnetism and has been studied with quantitative theory and spectroscopy. It has potential for spintronics, although devices are not yet established.
assessment.attribution: Pfleiderer's group provided the first observation in MnSi (neutron scattering, 2009) and Tokura's group the real-space Lorentz-TEM imaging in FeCoSi (2010); Wiesendanger's group showed atomic-scale spin-resolved STM skyrmion lattices at interfaces (2011). Theoretical origins by Bogdanov and Rossler-Bogdanov-Hubert are not in the credited names and are central to fair priority; Fert, Parkin and others also contributed to the interface and racetrack ideas.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by multiple independent techniques and in many materials, including room-temperature skyrmions. The application case remains unproven, so timing may be premature relative to technology impact.
uncertainties: Omission of Bogdanov and Fert from the credited set makes attribution uncertain.
Practical device relevance is unproven.
Priority among the 2009-2011 observations needs careful checking.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is the leading non-perturbative framework for strongly correlated electrons, exact in infinite dimensions, explaining the Mott transition and, via DFT+DMFT, giving quantitative material-specific spectra for correlated oxides, f-electron and transition-metal systems. This is close to my own interests, with direct ties to photoemission and spectroscopy.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimension limit (1989), Georges and Kotliar developed the mapping to an impurity problem (1992), and Kotliar led the DFT+DMFT realisation. Müller-Hartmann and Rozenberg also contributed, so there is a possible omission; the Georges-Kotliar-Vollhardt trio is a reasonable but not unique choice.
assessment.maturity: Over three decades of use and benchmarking, widely adopted and the interpretation is stable. Recognition is mature, though some may regard the topic as a method rather than a discovery of physical phenomena.
uncertainties: Whether a theoretical method qualifies as a discovery is a matter for committee judgement.
Quantitative accuracy for real materials depends on double-counting and interaction parameters, which remain somewhat ambiguous.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Giant room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions, first in amorphous alumina and then enormously enhanced in epitaxial MgO via coherent spin-dependent tunnelling, underlies read heads and MRAM. The physics of symmetry-filtered tunnelling is quantitatively predicted by first-principles theory (Butler, Mathon), a pleasing theory-experiment match.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera independently reported large room-temperature TMR in 1995; Yuasa and independently Parkin demonstrated coherent MgO tunnelling in 2004. Parkin is not in the supplied credit, and Butler and Mathon's theoretical predictions are also not credited, which weakens fairness of the configuration.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and technologically deployed. The close precedent of the 2007 GMR prize may reduce the perceived novelty, so timing is late but sound.
uncertainties: Absence of Parkin and theory contributors from the credit list.
Overlap with the GMR prize may make the Committee view this as an extension.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise the Hubbard model and its quantum phase transitions with controllable parameters, including the superfluid-Mott transition, and enable analogue quantum simulation of many-body physics. Conceptually significant for condensed-matter questions, with quantum microscopes giving single-site resolution.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Cirac (with Jaksch) proposed the lattice realisation; Greiner and Bloch performed the superfluid-Mott experiments and developed quantum gas microscopy. Hansch and Jaksch contributions are relevant but not credited. A three-person configuration of Bloch, Greiner and Zoller is plausible but Cirac's role is a clear competing claim.
assessment.maturity: Strong confirmation from many groups; the field is mature. Whether it has produced new physical insight beyond known models is debated, and the 2025-type prize emphasis on circuits shows interest in quantum devices.
uncertainties: Competing claims between Cirac and Zoller on the theory side.
Quantum-simulation advantages over classical computation remain to be demonstrated for the most interesting regimes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nd2Fe14B magnets are the strongest commercial permanent magnets and are central to wind turbines, electric vehicles and drives, so they matter for the sustainable energy transition. The discovery of the Nd2Fe14B phase is concrete and its intrinsic magnetic properties are well understood from electronic-structure theory; this fits the Prize's tradition of valuing an invention with real use.
assessment.attribution: Sagawa (Sumitomo, sintered route) and Croat (General Motors, melt-spun route) announced the material independently in 1983-84, with Herbst's crystal structure and magnetism work also important. Two laureates are the natural fair configuration from the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Entirely mature and widely deployed, with decades of confirmation. The Nobel Committee has historically leaned toward fundamental discovery over materials engineering, so fit is uncertain.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee views this as sufficiently fundamental physics rather than materials engineering.
Herbst and others on the structure are outside the supplied credit.
Dependence on rare earths is a sustainability concern, though not a barrier to the scientific merit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Altermagnetism is a proposed third class of collinear magnetism with compensated order but spin-split bands from crystal symmetry, with promise for spintronics without stray fields. It is a conceptually clean new symmetry-based classification that electronic-structure theory predicts well, and I find it close to my own field.
assessment.attribution: Šmejkal, Sinova and Jungwirth articulated the classification and developed predictions (2019-2022), with several other groups (including Hayami, Yuan, Mazin) making overlapping contributions in the same period. The credited trio is plausible but credit allocation is still unsettled.
assessment.maturity: Experimental confirmation (ARPES and other probes in MnTe, CrSb, and others) arrived in 2024, so it is very recent and probably premature for a prize.
uncertainties: Recent experimental confirmation, with limited independent replication so far.
Priority disputes with other groups who proposed related ideas.
Practical device demonstrations are lacking.
